tagline: The Netherlands' southern jewel has Roman roots, a bookstore inside a 13th-century church, caves under Mount Saint Peter and a Burgundian love of food.
overview: Maastricht sits on the Maas River in the far south, squeezed between Belgium and Germany, and it feels quite different from the rest of the country: hilly, French-tinged and devoted to good food. It is one of the oldest cities in the Netherlands, with Roman foundations and medieval walls.

The Vrijthof square is framed by the Basilica of Saint Servatius and St John's Church, and Dominicanen bookshop fills a converted 13th-century Gothic church. The Sint Servaasbrug, one of the oldest bridges in the country, links the old town to the Wyck district.

Under Sint-Pietersberg hill, centuries of marlstone quarrying left a maze of caves that served as shelters in wartime, and guided tours lead through them. In 1992 the Maastricht Treaty, which created the European Union, was signed here, and the city's carnival is the liveliest in the country.
